newsitem.title: GERMANY: Still no deal on new German tax rates - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Still no deal on new German tax rates - Waigel.

text.p: A German government tax policy group, meeting for the penultimate time before it is due to complete a major reform plan next week, failed on Monday to agree on new income tax rates to take effect in 1999.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said after his coalition's tax commission met that two proposals were still being discussed -- sticking to the current straight-line sliding scale for income taxes, or creating a stepped system of three tax brackets.
Big income tax cuts are the centrepiece of a reform bid by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government to simplify the tax system, cut tax evasion and give the unemployment-hit economy a boost.

Waigel said that the entry tax rate was likely to be 20 percent or below, down from the current 26 percent. But he did not say what the top rate, currently 53 percent, would be. In the past, he has said the top rate would be cut below 40 percent.

Both Waigel, who favours the linear system, and leaders from junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), who back a simpler three-tier concept, said the financial impact of their proposals would be similar.
"This is not a matter of faith," Waigel told reporters.

Reductions in taxes on income, company profits and interest earnings should lower the tax load by 70 billion marks. The commission has already agreed on scrapping 33 billion marks in tax breaks to partly offset the cuts, Waigel said.
He has said he is seeking a net tax cut of 30 billion marks -- leaving the remainder likely to be covered by increasing Germany's relatively low 15 percent rate of value-added tax.

Waigel said that the question of taxing pensions had still not yet been decided, and would be addressed at a joint meeting of the tax panel and a pensions reform working group headed by Social Security Minister Norbert Bluem.
Final decisions on the tax reform package are planned to be made at a meeting on January 23, ushering in a consultative political process which Kohl has said could take all year.
